title: test-0056-SCI-PHY-MOTION9
passage: To understand motion, we must distinguish between distance and displacement. Distance is the total path length covered, while displacement is the shortest straight-line distance from the initial to the final position. If an athlete runs a full lap around a circular track and returns to the starting point, their displacement is zero, even though they have covered a significant distance. Motion also involves speed and velocity. Speed is simply how fast an object moves, but velocity is speed in a specific direction. Therefore, an object moving at a constant speed in a circle has a changing velocity because its direction constantly shifts. This change in velocity means the object is accelerating, even if its speed remains steady. Furthermore, acceleration is not just speeding up; it is any change in velocity over time. If a car slows down while moving forward, it is undergoing negative acceleration, or deceleration. Finally, when analyzing motion using graphs, a horizontal line on a velocity-time graph indicates that the velocity is constant, not that the object is at rest. The area under this velocity-time graph represents the total displacement of the object, not a physical surface area. Understanding these distinctions helps us describe motion accurately without confusing scalar quantities with vector quantities.
